title: The Sublime Somi Bridges African and Western Jazz
author: @NewYorker
content:
Also: David Greenspan and Lupita Nyong’o onstage, the found-object art of Narcissister, a Hong Kong-born filmmaker’s exploration of family history, and more.

September 25, 2026

In the past two decades, the singer Laura Kabasomi Kakoma, who performs music mononymously as Somi, has become a bridge between Western jazz and the jazz of Africa. An Illinois-born New Yorker of Rwandan and Ugandan descent who grew up in Zambia, she channels her diasporic upbringing into a synergized and singular sound—one anchored by a lovely, fluid voice that is paradoxically both calm and emphatic. She collaborated with the distinguished South African trumpeter Hugh Masekela, helped relaunch Sony’s Okeh Records as a jazz label, and released a tribute album for the singer-songwriter and activist Miriam Makeba. In 2021, Somi became the first African woman nominated in a jazz category at the Grammys.

Somi’s work is possessed by its duty to multiple traditions, something the singer has referred to as trying to “tell the truth” of her “dual inheritance.” Her songs have a stateliness to them, and yet they are unrestricted in their pursuit of a nuanced pan-African modality, the stories and rhythms at play therein. The 2014 album “The Lagos Music Salon” sought to embody the magic of the titular city, the result of an intracontinental cultural migration. Its 2017 follow-up, “Petite Afrique,” was even more ambitious: the song cycle deployed her sublime voice in search of answers for the African immigrants of Harlem as gentrification threatened the community they had built. Somi is also a playwright and actress; she wrote and starred in the Off Broadway musical “Dreaming Zenzile,” about Makeba, and starred, on Broadway, in “Jaja’s African Hair Braiding.” Her new album, “What Does It Take to Bloom?,” is a journey inward. Produced with Benjamin James, of the Nigerian highlife band the Cavemen, it is the most poised record of her career, and she brings its songs, and those of her many musical expeditions, to Sony Hall, on Oct. 1.—Sheldon Pearce

Off Broadway

Marin Ireland’s semi-autobiographical play “Pre-Existing Condition” stars a vivid Lupita Nyong’o as A (the casting will rotate), whose world is reeling with confusion and shame following an incident in which her former boyfriend hit her so hard that she ended up on the floor. (She had tried to slap him a few days before, she offers wanly.) In impressionistic sketches, directed by Maria Dizzia, A struggles through sessions with a therapist (the appealingly forthright Dael Orlandersmith), group counselling (facilitated by the cheeky Sarah Steele and Orlandersmith), a date (Greg Keller, a nuanced charmer), her clueless mother (also Keller). She connects with a guy friend who respects her boundaries—after which, in a fraught meeting with her absentee father, A takes a step in a suddenly clear, positive direction.—Shauna Lyon (Greenwich House Theatre; through Jan. 8.)

Off Off Broadway

Tom Stoppard’s “The Invention of Love” opens with the freshly dead classicist and poet A. E. Housman (a singsongy David Greenspan) reminiscing about his days at Oxford, astir with fin-de-siècle aestheticism and the titillations of his fellow-undergraduate Oscar Wilde (Sam Bolen, transfixing in this role and two others). But the young Housman (Yaron Lotan) took more interest in another student, the strapping Moses Jackson (José Espinosa), for whom his feelings were epitomized by the bond between Achilles and Patroclus, and between other close-knit comrades of antiquity, the field to which he devoted himself. Stoppard’s allusiveness is daunting but rewarding—something recognized by the director, Zachary Elkind, whose low-tech but resourceful staging refuses to pander.—Dan Stahl (Theaterlab; through Oct. 3.)

Dance

The Gulf of Mexico may not be the first place one thinks of in relation to the ballet choreographers Frederick Ashton and Antony Tudor, and yet the excellent Sarasota Ballet has made itself a bastion of the twentieth-century British ballet repertoire. The troupe has also recently taken on several new dancers, including the princely Andrii Ishchuk, lately of American Ballet Theatre. On the program is Tudor’s moving portrait of repressed love and grim marital convention, “Lilac Garden”; the devilishly difficult balcony scene from Ashton’s “Romeo and Juliet,” with lots of tricky hopping on pointe; and the bucolic Peter Wright quartet “Summertide,” set to the shimmering second movement of Mendelssohn’s Second Piano Concerto.—Marina Harss (Joyce Theatre; Sept. 29-Oct. 4.)

Pop

The chronically online pop-music fan is obsessive about positioning relative to the market—terms such as “flop era” and “Khia asylum” dominating their conversations about recognition and artistry—and few musicians have been more subject to this discourse than Slayyyter. A viral sensation in the halcyon days of Twitter, the singer was on the forefront of a sleaze-pop revival, and her self-titled 2019 mixtape, which found her at the intersection of the dance pop of the mid-two-thousands and the hyperpop still to come, put her on the shortlist of stars-to-be. When that call didn’t arrive, even Slayyyter questioned her career path, and she planned her March album, “Wor$t Girl in America,” as if it were her last, writing an ode to her iPod. Ironically, in doubling down on herself, she has never been more popular.—Sheldon Pearce (Terminal 5; Oct. 3. Brooklyn Paramount; Oct. 4.)

Art

For nearly two decades, the artist Narcissister has developed a body of work marked by evocative visual motifs: an idealized feminine face mask, maneuvers involving contortion or sleight of hand, and nudity (her merkin is as common a sight as her mask). Her performances, which mischievously shred expectations of gender and race, have taken place in night clubs and at art museums—and on the TV show “America’s Got Talent.” For this exhibition, she constructed an installation out of found objects which doubles as a Rube Goldberg machine. Amid ropes, barrels, and exercise balls lies the show’s emotional core: seascapes painted by her uncle. She honors them, and a complex family legacy, in her indelibly risqué way, in a handful of performances, during which she wears her aunt’s dresses.—Jillian Steinhauer (Margot Samel; through Oct. 10.)

Movies

In “Palimpsest: The Story of a Name,” the filmmaker Mary Stephen, a Hong Kong-born, ethnic-Chinese filmmaker, indeed explores the mystery of her own name. Her fascinating, playful quest involves the tangled background of her father, Henry Stephen. After his death, in 1986, she discovered a trove of his diaristic writings and home movies; with these archives she reconstructs his life and her childhood. The film unfolds his rough-and-tumble youth in Hong Kong; the turmoil of the Second World War; her father’s successful career in business; his encounter with the filmmaker’s mother, who called herself Hilda; and widespread divisions of class and race. The resulting stories involve surprising intersections of family and politics, of identity and imagination.—Richard Brody (Streaming on OVID.tv.)

Ryan Gellis discovers a beer counter in South Slope.

In sleepy South Slope, a local son in search of a beer bar walked past a familiar, long-shuttered laundromat. He did a double take—the rusting metal window grates were gone, the hulking coin-operated machines nowhere in sight, but an enticing sign had appeared on the awning: “BEER COUNTER.” Inside, people were still dealing in suds, albeit of a different kind. Mash Inn had transformed into an airy space, with a blond-wood bar and a forest of potted plants. Sixteen bronze taps stood ready to dispense craft ales, lagers, and a single cider. The patron chose a Cultivar: Cascade, from Wayward Lane Brewing, a hazy pale ale whose tiny bubbles effervesced so vigorously as to mist the upper lip. Two other townies were spotted, and their table was joined. These malt maestros, noting the surrounding mature crowd, wondered about the purported demise of drinking culture while they crunched through a bowl of puffed-rice snacks. The Mash Inn is a relative of the established brewski mecca Gold Star Beer Counter, in Prospect Heights, and has a similarly minimalist menu. In place of a liquor shelf (the establishment sells only beer and cider), there’s a turntable and a library of vinyl—this evening’s up-tempo jazz struggled to compete with the din of a full house. The next round was on the latecomer; a wild ale by the name of Arietta, from Fox Farm Brewery, floral and largely flat, had a pleasing barnyard funk. A Subglitch sour was rechristened “Jolly Rancher light.” It was conceded that the catalogue of brews outmatched the finite power of the liver. Upon decampment, the drowsy drinker is met with one final chance to imbibe, at the outside window, its sliding partition reminiscent of a Mister Softee’s. A growler of stout makes for pleasant company on the walk home.

P.S. Good stuff on the internet:

  • Designing the commonplace
  • How Leonard Cohen smelled
  • Victor Garber’s life-changing Jesus

  • Parents disagreed on whether to vaccinate their children. Then the kids got sick.

Sheldon Pearce is a music writer for The New Yorker’s Goings On newsletter.

Dan Stahl is a member of The New Yorker’s editorial staff.

Jillian Steinhauer received a 2023 Rabkin Prize for visual-arts writing. She teaches in the Journalism and Design program at the New School.

title: Still On Its Way to Cleveland
author: Betsy Blondin
content:
Thoughtful stories for thoughtless times.

Longreads has published hundreds of original stories—personal essays, reported features, reading lists, and more—and more than 14,000 editor’s picks. And they’re all funded by readers like you. Become a member today.

Mark and Betsy Blondin | Longreads | September 22, 2026 | 2,702 words (10 minutes)

We left Boyne City, Michigan, in the fall of 1996 in a 34-foot Coachmen motorhome towing a minivan, with three children, a golden retriever not originally part of the plan, and a desktop computer on a stand bolted to the floor where a chair used to be. We stopped in Flint to say goodbye to family and retrofit the motorhome for the road. Mark’s father had died that June. His mother was devastated, and for a while the question wasn’t which route to choose but whether to go at all. We left Flint on October 4. Five miles later, the motorhome shut down.

A loose fuel line.

A few miles after the fuel line was fixed, we were surprised by a flat tire on the van’s tow dolly, and then, unbelievably, we bent a bumper while putting the van back on the dolly. It was past seven in the evening. We were finally on our way to Cleveland, Ohio.

That was day one. What we built over the following nine months—25,000 miles through 40 states—would go on to earn a Yahoo! Cool Site designation, a presentation at a US Department of Education national conference, and a place in the federal Education Resources Information Center archive. On the road, we filed over 1,500 emails and website dispatches from museum lobbies, hotel reception desks, libraries, and wherever we could find a phone jack and someone willing to let us run a telephone cord to their wall.

Google would not exist for another two years. The word “blog” had not yet been coined. We were doing something that had no name and no manual, and we were doing it over a dial-up modem while living in a motorhome.

Blondins’ Assignment America was both the name of our trip and the website we built in real time as we traveled. We had a partnership with Northwest Academy, a science and technology charter school in northern Michigan in its first year of operation, that made it possible. We had prepared to make the case for why our children—Donald, 14, and twins Kelly and Stacy, 11—would not attend the 1996–97 school year in a conventional sense. The school board didn’t just accommodate us; they encouraged us. Northwest Academy loaned us a laptop and a 1.2 MP digital camera, and we took their curriculum on the road.

The idea had been circulating for some time. For over a year, we had been looking at our future and considering ideas for our next step. Watching The Bridges of Madison County and the questions it raises about the road not taken confirmed for us that we could do something unconventional and educational. Our adventure was also, after Mark’s 12-year career run at Coca-Cola, exactly what we needed.

Red flags of risk waved. In Betsy’s 1996 site bio before the trip began, she wrote her own reasons for going: “I hope [the children] learn that although it is not always easy, unconventional choices in life can be made. Quitting my part-time job as a writer for The Citizen in Boyne City for this adventure was not easy for me. Neither is the financial risk, but I believe it will be worth it.”

What emerged was a family travel journal published to the web, which we updated continuously with photographs and written dispatches. On the site we invited visitors to submit their own travel stories and organically grew a readership we couldn’t really see or measure. Blondins’ Assignment America, our family’s online home, resided at blondins.com, running on Microsoft FrontPage 97.

It is still there. We have not updated the code. The link list on the homepage points to AltaVista, HotBot, and WebCrawler. Many of the links are broken. It is an archive, broken links and all—a well-preserved time capsule.

This archive holds more than our travel dispatches. Each family member had their own web page. Donald created Donald.com on GeoCities, a web hosting service that allowed users to create and publish websites for free. He dated his site-building career to November 27, 1996—54 days into the trip. One section with links to tutorials existed to teach strangers how to build websites of their own. The note for November 18, 1997, reads: “I have photoshop! Major site changes are coming.” 

The photographs were 640 by 480 pixels, because anything larger would take a reader minutes to load; we could feel our audience’s patience through the phone line. We uploaded our dispatches whenever we could find a connection—this fundamental part of our publishing process was not on a schedule, nor was it guaranteed. Seven weeks in, parked in Sarasota, Florida, Mark wrote in his journal that he hoped to get something on the site before we left. The week before, in Jacksonville, three days had passed with no update.

When we were lucky, we were able to upload our accounts of adventures on the day they happened.

Stacy posted on October 15, 1996: “Dear Journal: Today was not my favorite day, but it was okay. We spent half the day looking for a place to check our e-mail and were successful. Then we went to the Portland Museum of Art where we saw some neat artwork by Winslow Homer, Andrew Wyeth, etc. Later that night we went swimming while Dad and Donald went to Maine Internet Connections. Kelly and I had lots of fun playing at the pool. We slept once again at the college police parking lot.”

Kelly wrote about our hike on the Lost Mine Trail in the Chisos Mountains of Big Bend National Park in Texas on January 9, 1997. “The trail was supposedly five and a half miles, but straight uphill. We made it back down in about 45 minutes. When we got back, we did some laundry. For dinner, we had barbecue chicken in tortilla shells. There was still snow on the Chisos. There is a legend that there is gold in the mountain.”

Our stories traveled unfiltered into the world for anyone anywhere to read. 

In our 34-foot home, the dinette was the flat surface where we spread out school work and projects and wrote in our journals. It also converted to a bed for Donald. When he wanted to sleep before the rest of us, the cry went out to clear the dinette—a plea or a command, depending on the night. Years later we could still hear echoes of “clear the dinette!”

The web of 1996 was not yet monetized in the way it is today. The internet then wasn’t flooded with platforms competing for your attention and harvesting and selling your data, or algorithms constantly tuned to optimize for engagement. At the time, Yahoo! had editors—actual people employed to look at websites and decide which ones were worth surfacing to other people. That web lasted about a decade before it was dismantled, piece by piece, in favor of one that extracts profits from similar interactions. 

We were the beneficiaries of that architecture and didn’t know it was temporary.

Logistics in the physical world were more challenging than in the world online. Six weeks in, we were low on propane, parked in a friend’s driveway in Maplewood, New Jersey, taking the van into New York City on day trips. The only place that filled RV tanks was in Jersey City. We left the van behind and drove the motorhome onto streets built for nothing that long. Following sketchy directions, we stopped several times to ask for help. The horns behind us did not let up. We found the place, got the propane, and worked our way back through the traffic.

It was one of the worst days of our trip. 

Some of our best days resulted from meeting people while finding ways to get online. Back on day one at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History, we told our story, and after a momentary pause, the receptionist at the information desk gave us her chair. We sat at her desk in that major museum and filed our dispatches while visitors walked up to ask for directions to the dinosaurs. We did our best to help. 

The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, also in Cleveland, gave us free admission, a press kit, and a phone line. The Great Lakes Science Center nearby, and new that year, gave us free admission and a tour by their PR director. We got better at telling the story, and three charming children helped.

A man named Pierre at a Portland, Maine, YMCA spent an hour trying every phone line in the building to help us connect.

In New York City, our communication efforts found us, just a bit embarrassed, walking down the aisle in our travel clothes to seats five rows from the stage at The King and I. Mark had called the box office that afternoon and told a woman named Sandy our story. Our tickets were waiting at will call for a magical theater night.

A 7-Eleven outside Washington, DC, became a nightly ritual: We’d run a 50-foot cord to the backroom, upload the day’s pages, check and send email, and play a trivia game about the museums we’d visited. Correct answers were worth a Slurpee. That is what the technology was for.

Somewhere past the Four Corners Monument on the Navajo Nation, we ran out of gas less than a mile short of a station that had no can to sell us. A man drove past, saw our motorhome stopped on the shoulder, and turned around. He went home for a gas can and brought back enough gas for us to reach the pump. We never learned his name. This is what human kindness did.

Betsy filed a few freelance columns for The Citizen from the road. Her parents mailed printed issues of the newspaper to whatever general-delivery post office or friend’s or relative’s address we could predict two weeks ahead.

The yeses got bigger as the trip went on. At the JFK Presidential Library outside of Boston, which also gave us free admission, Mark asked if we could park the motorhome in the lot overnight. The staff said yes, and after our visit they showed us where to park and locked the gate behind us. One family, one motorhome, one golden retriever, inside the locked grounds of a federal presidential library, with a view of Boston in the dark. Nobody had a policy for that. Someone had a key and decided yes.

When we needed someone to take Buddy for the month we spent in Hawaii, we found him a home through a golden retriever email list. It connected us to a breeder in Morton, Washington, who knew a young man near Seattle raising his own golden for a 4-H project. He needed the money; Buddy needed a yard. The family also had room for the motorhome. Nobody took a percentage. Nobody optimized the match.

No matter where we were, the realities of our past intruded on our adventure. The family parked the motorhome in Pacifica, California, and waited while Mark flew back to Michigan. He had been fired by Coca-Cola Enterprises in March 1995, and his age-discrimination suit had reached the deposition stage. It ran from nine in the morning to 5:30 p.m. His mother waited at the house our family still owned but no longer lived in. With the retirement savings spent down, much was dependent on the court case going well.

We returned home in June 1997, rich in experience and financially broke. A brief exchange at a campground became an unforgettable memory. Betsy had told an elderly man she was worried the children wouldn’t understand or appreciate what the trip had been. He thought about it. “Maybe it’s not a matter of appreciating it as something unique or separate,” he told her. “It will simply become part of who they are.”  

We spent the summer running an ice cream and yogurt business, and planning the future. While researching, we discovered a request for abstracts from the organizers of a US Department of Education conference called “Families, Technology, and Education.” We were accepted as featured speakers and off to Chicago that October.

A PowerPoint to help tell our story and a video our children had made in Big Bend National Park on its plant and animal life fit the conference title in every way. On a stage in front of 400 educators from around the country, we made our presentation. During the Q&A period, Donald fielded several questions like a pro. Our paper, People Make Dreams Come True, and Technology Expands the Possibilities: An Educational Journey across the United States, seemed close to becoming a template for the future of education—and we had played a role.

In June 1998, an email arrived from a stranger in New York.

His name was Ted Sammons, and he worked in the editorial department of Broadway Books. He had seen Blondins’ Assignment America on Yahoo!’s “Cool Site” listing and had been impressed—and, he admitted, a bit jealous. He believed the story of our trip would make a good book, and he wanted to know if we’d thought about writing one. Of course we had.

We made our pitch, but ultimately, the editorial board passed. Their stated reason was not enough tragedy. 

In 1998, our story was: family leaves, family travels, family lands well. We both began new careers. It’s an adventure with an enviable ending. Eventually, Donald went to Berkeley, and Kelly and Stacy went to Harvard.

In December 1997, we put the Boyne City house on the market, loaded the motorhome for its last trip, and landed in Carlsbad, California, one of our favorite cities discovered on our journey. It was there that Betsy began work as a managing editor and Mark went into the technology industry. Our children thrived. 

A decade passed, and the publisher Betsy worked for went under. Cloud computing came for the company Mark worked for, and then for the storage business he started. In 2009, we lost our Carlsbad house.

Getting from Carlsbad to a city on the Portuguese coast took 10 more years and three continents worth of seeking. But that isn’t this story.

Today, the children are grown and our family is scattered across four countries. The household that once ran a 50-foot cord into a 7-Eleven backroom to send the day’s mail now talks on platforms that eavesdrop on what we say.

Our children’s dispatches still live where they filed them, and how they perceive the trip is not a question we have to ask in 2026. We see it in them. In their curiosity, courage, and adaptability that can partly be traced back to Cleveland. The older, wise man at the campground had predicted correctly. It has indeed become a part of each of us.

Recently, we went looking for who still visits the site. The statistics page is a dead link; it has outlived the instrument that measured it.

We both still write, and Betsy still edits, from a town on the Portuguese coast—a domain renewed annually, hosting billed monthly, a newsletter on a platform that takes its percentage. Every function we had for free in 1996, now itemized. The North Central Michigan College server had hosted our website and asked for nothing.  

While the early web afforded us online advantages, the real-world experiences and connections we enjoyed would not have been possible without the human kindness and generosity we found along the way. Both human and online access made our adventure possible.

Our story is a record of an internet that no longer exists: the one with human editors, not algorithms, discovering and surfacing content worth seeing. The one that offered real access and possibility, resulting in a federal agency highlighting our work and an editor at a major publishing house discovering our project. The one that connected us to a host family for our dog and motorhome in rural Washington, no strings attached. That internet—serendipitous, kind, free, and open—is gone.

Nine months, 25,000 miles, 40 states. Three kids who were there for all of it. A golden retriever who died years later in Carlsbad. A motorhome that is long gone. 

And a website that is, in the most literal sense, still on its way to Cleveland.

Mark and Betsy Blondin are living and writing in Vila do Conde, Portugal, currently at work on a memoir of the thirty years that followed Assignment America. Betsy is a longtime writer and editor at WordMetro.com who compiled and published Migraine Expressions: A Creative Journey Through Life with Migraine. Together, they published At Home Abroad: Today’s Expats Tell Their Stories. Mark’s work has appeared in The Humanist, and he writes at markblondin.com and Material Witness.

title: He Was One of the World’s Most Wanted Men. So He Bought a West African Country.
author: Seyward Darby
content:
Just a few years ago, Jos Leijdekkers was a gangster in Antwerp, working for a major drug lord. Today he’s the most powerful man in Sierra Leone, which he’s single-handedly turned into a crucial port in the transatlantic cocaine trade. European authorities haven’t been able to track him down. Can a journalist? Alexander Clapp details Leijdekkers’s remarkable, violent rise to power, while looking for the man himself:

“These kinds of people, we are always seeing them in Africa. They come, they disappear. But the moment we learned who he was, it freaked me out,” a local car-dealer who was one of the first people to sell a motor to Leijdekkers, told me. “I left Sierra Leone after finding out. I became really scared. Not small scared.” Sophie van Leeuwen, a Dutch correspondent for RTL News, told me she “had the strong feeling I was being followed by the secret police” during the first days of a reporting trip she took to Sierra Leone in February 2025. She was arrested outside a villa where Leijdekkers was believed to reside, informed that she had intruded upon a “special security situation”, and questioned for 15 hours. Her camera and computer were searched and scrubbed. The Flemish owner of her hotel was interrogated over her alleged role in seeding a European spy network in Sierra Leone.

One evening in the hills above Freetown I attended a cocktail party where Western diplomats mingled with aid-workers. “Careful with that,” a European mission head told me when I mentioned why I had come to Africa, swivelling her blue eyes round the room. A Norwegian mining investor assured me that there would only be one way of knowing whether I was making progress in my investigation: “The government will arrange a car crash for you.”

title: Where Cities and Oceans Meet
author: Cheri Lucas Rowlands
content:
What does it mean to live in a disappearing place? For Pioneer Works’ Broadcast, Brad Bolman, a professor of history and environmental studies at Tulane University, writes about New Orleans, the shifting borders between land and sea, and the political and economic forces that continue to shape the city’s fate in a time of climate catastrophe.

If Los Angeles is the city that has been imaginatively destroyed again and again in film and TV, as Thom Andersen argues in Los Angeles Plays Itself, New Orleans is the one that has been destroyed countless times in reality. We have survived worse and rebuilt before, many insisted. We’re staying.

It was a reaction as understandable emotionally as it was disconnected from environmental reality. But that gap is a feature of life in the Crescent City. As I watched my first Mardi Gras parade this spring, junk falling in never-ending torrents from brightly decorated floats, a friend sympathetically interjected, “This must be driving you crazy.” What they meant was that as someone who teaches about environmental history but isn’t from here, I must be especially affected by the throwaway culture of the city’s most famous fête and its tons and tons of plastic beads, made from the same fossil fuels that are causing sea levels to rise around us.

title: Two cheers for “insecure originalism”
author: Richard Re
content:
In his new book, Justice Samuel Alito takes aim at what he calls judicial “insecurity,” or a judge’s self-conscious worry that he might be advancing his own policy preferences under the guise of impartial adjudication. “Twenty-first century originalists,” he argues, “should shed this insecure mindset.”

Alito’s suggestion is at odds with decades of conservative legal thought, including remarks by Justice Antonin Scalia. More fundamentally, what Alito labels insecurity is better understood as a form of humility and self-awareness. And that humility is laudable for all judges, not just originalists. There is much more to fear from the self-assured or overconfident judge than the insecure one.

Was Scalia “insecure”?

In some of the book’s most discussed passages (and in an op-ed in The Wall Street Journal), Alito impugns “insecure originalism,” in part because “insecurity” may lead originalists “to worry that they are subconsciously engaging in ‘results-oriented’ decision-making and ‘judicial activism’ in the service of their own policy preferences.” Alito urges originalists to shrug off this worry: “Originalist judges should . . . be on guard against subconsciously setting a higher bar for legal arguments that yield outcomes they find desirable as a policy matter.”

The insecurity that Alito bemoans has a rich history that his discussion omits. In recent decades, the jurist most associated with this kind of thinking was longtime conservative hero Scalia. In his oft-repeated view, “The judge who always likes the results he reaches is a bad judge.” This maxim was admonitory. It not so subtly suggested that other judges, perhaps of the non-originalist variety, always liked where their theorizing led them. But not the principled originalist, whose impartial theory necessarily brought about disappointment – the price of integrity.

Scalia often fleshed out this line of thinking by pointing to specific issues that originalism resolved in ways he claimed to find regrettable. The First Amendment, in Scalia’s view, encompassed a right to burn the American flag, something that Scalia personally found distasteful. And the confrontation clause effectively demanded that many serious offenders go unpunished. Scalia’s critics sometimes chafed when he drew attention to these decisions, which seemed to give him permission to issue other rulings that did align with his own policy preferences.

Scalia’s disciples have long echoed his view of the “bad judge.” In published writings, including a judicial opinion, Justice Neil Gorsuch has favorably adapted Scalia’s “bad judge” admonition. And Justice Amy Coney Barrett made Scalia’s aphorism a prominent part of her recent memoir and related book tour. Barrett has also offered her own variations on this theme, remarking for instance: “You should sometimes be reaching results that you really dislike.” In a similar spirit, a majority opinion by Justice Brett Kavanaugh defended its own impartiality by adducing examples of standing decisions that cut in different ideological directions.

Insecurity, or anti-partisanship?

What Alito labels “insecurity” is really a judicial virtue and better characterized as a form of self-consciousness or rigor. When a judge realizes that he is consistently ruling for or against a particular kind of party, he has good reason to reflect on the possibility that he is the victim of his own biases. That point has special salience in today’s United States, which is marked by partisan polarization.

When a judge confronts a case with partisan valence, he would do well to pause over his own potential bias. In the context of contemporary federal judging, such a bias often correlates with the judge’s appointing president. A judge appointed by a Republican or Democratic president is likely to have personal views aligned with Republicans or Democrats, respectively. And the judge is likely to have a social set that is ideologically skewed. As Alito noted in an interview, such a skew may not be the judge’s doing, so much as the result of ideological backlash against the judge’s rulings. But even if unfair or unfortunate, the backlash’s effects are real.

In this context, a judge will be tempted to please his own ideological tribe while being insensitive to its rival. A Democratic-appointed judge may play to Bluesky, writing zingers in trendy language that please imagined audiences. Or a Republican-appointed judge may similarly look forward to standing ovations at Federalist Society galas. These incentives and trains of thought are not so hypothetical. And once this kind of behavior takes hold, the judges in question become more like partisan actors than principled defenders of either legal rules or the judiciary.

Against that backdrop, an anti-partisanship principle offers a means of reaching better, more accurate results – not a means of sacrificing accuracy for illicit ends. A judge who sensibly factors in his own partisan affiliation, background, or associations is more likely to identify and apply the law by his own lights. Or so one might hope. Whether anti-partisanship can work largely depends on how it is implemented.

Implementing anti-partisanship

There are many ways of implementing anti-partisanship, and different approaches may befit different scenarios or appeal to different jurists. Surely no judge should factor in party identity in a way that squarely contradicts the law’s dictates. And because many judges have sincere legal views with an ideological valence, complete anti-partisanship is both infeasible and undesirable. Yet judging often involves subtle choices. And those subtleties create room for the anti-partisanship principle to have meaningful effect.

At the Supreme Court, certiorari, that is, deciding what case to hear, affords perhaps the most immediate opportunity for discretionary judgments. Is a particular case or issue ripe for prompt consideration, or sufficiently worthy of the court’s attention? These questions yield judgment calls, and a judge may reasonably consider whether he is consistently making these decisions in favor of one party or ideology. Cert might be warranted only when a relatively objective test is satisfied, such as a deep circuit split. Or the justice might have a practice of avoiding expedited review in such cases.

Moreover, all appellate courts confront myriad opportunities to craft the scope and depth of their holdings. A judge who supports one broad holding after another in favor of his appointing president or party is probably ruling irresponsibly. That judge is not merely transgressing principles of minimalism (deciding only what needs to be decided) or gradualism (deciding incrementally) but doing so in an especially objectionable way by ruling grandly with partisan effect. By contrast, a humbler judge will be sure to wait beyond the first or second chance to resolve a major issue when that issue has a partisan valence.

Judges of all kinds also face an array of different grounds on which to rule. An anti-partisan judge might look with care at jurisdictional requirements or opportunities for abstention, adapting Alexander Bickel’s “passive virtues” (that is, pursuing an impassive strategy, rather than ruling either swiftly or grandly). Or he might shelve a holding in the alternative where a single, narrower holding would suffice.

Precedent affords additional opportunities for anti-partisanship. When a party seeks to overrule case law, a judge might ask whether that request has a partisan valence – and then look to see whether the request to overrule has broad, cross-ideological support.

Finally, judges may express themselves differently depending on the presence of partisan tensions. Barrett made this point in Trump v. Anderson, which (as to result) unanimously held that Colorado could not exclude then-candidate Trump from the presidential ballot based on section 3 of the 14th Amendment. She wrote separately to note that the court “has settled a politically charged issue in the volatile season of a Presidential election” and that, “[p]articularly in this circumstance, writings on the Court should turn the national temperature down, not up.” Thus, Anderson was “not the time to amplify disagreement with stridency.” In other contexts, judges may follow this general advice by muting their rhetoric or even suppressing dissents.

Too anti-partisan?

In our current polarized environment, it may be hard to imagine that a judge would be too anti-partisan. Yet Alito quite properly raises just that concern.

As Alito insightfully puts it: “insecure originalists may actually welcome occasions when their originalist analysis leads to results they dislike. When that occurs, they experience a gratifying frisson, a brief catharsis in which their anxiety about having unconsciously succumbed to the temptation of results-oriented decision-making is released.” The image here is of a judge who becomes so excited about proving his own impartiality that he becomes utterly partial.

Once again, Alito’s point is hardly limited to originalists, and other commentators have raised similar concerns about judging in general. For example, Judge Richard Posner once noted that “[i]t is a source of satisfaction to a judge to vote for the litigant who irritates him . . . for it is by doing such things that you know that you are playing the judge role.”

This kind of concern shows that the anti-partisanship principle must itself be deployed reflectively and cautiously. There is no one simple trick for impartial or accurate judging, and any maxim of juridical wisdom can be twisted or taken too much to heart.

Alito’s worry also indicates that the anti-partisanship principle has only contingent appeal. In a less polarized polity, partisanship might play a smaller or even a trivial role in judicial decision-making. In that environment, the anti-partisanship principle would not help – or might even worsen – judicial bias. But that is not our world today.

Alito elaborates his point in a way that further underscores the appeal of anti-partisanship. To wit, he notes that “an originalist judge should not cavalierly or happily embrace results that defy common sense.” Attention to common sense is indeed justifiable, but that is because (or if) it is truly “common.” Consensus views may well provide a helpful indication that a particular ruling is senseless, catastrophic, or absurd.

But “common sense” is not at all the same as Alito’s other and more salient subject – namely, “outcomes [judges] find desirable as a policy matter.” In placing these two ideas in successive paragraphs and casting them as comparable, Alito inadvertently reveals how easy it is for a judge to draw an equivalence between, or fail to differentiate, his own highly contestable views and genuine consensus.

Anti-partisanship may not be for everyone. The legal system may even benefit from having some judges in each court who align with one or the other of the nation’s two political parties. That arrangement would help partisans identify with the judiciary and might foster a kind of adversarial system within the third branch. But that picture seems appealing, if at all, only if the partisan judges remain the exception.

“The Spirit of Liberty”

In a later chapter, Alito praises Judge Learned Hand’s famous speech on “the Spirit of Liberty.” Alito notes for instance: “I am convinced that the spirit of the Constitution—of limited but effective government, individual rights, and equal justice under law—is alive and well in the hearts of the American people.”

Alas, Alito’s discussion does not quote or acknowledge what Hand believed the spirit of liberty to be. In the speech’s most memorable and oft-repeated line, Hand posited: “The spirit of liberty is the spirit which is not too sure that it is right.”

One might say that the spirit of liberty is a bit insecure. The spirit of the Constitution is, too.

title: How Jim Morrison Surmounted Tragedy and Skied Down Everest
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
Jim Morrison has endured almost unimaginable loss—first his wife and two young children in a plane crash, then his partner and climbing companion Hilaree Nelson in a Himalayan avalanche. But rather than stepping back from danger, he kept pursuing ever more risky objectives, culminating in the first ski descent of Everest’s nearly unclimbable north face via the Super Direct route. This profile explores Morrison’s perseverance and shows how, for some people, a life defined by extreme risk can never be retreated from.

“It was a profound, transformational moment for me to know that when I found Hilaree, she wasn’t in her body,” Morrison told me. “I dug her out of the snow. I held her in my arms. I screamed, and I cried, but it was just her dead body. She was no longer there, and it was as clear as anything has been in my entire lifetime. I had been haunted so much by my wife and my children, and what state they were in when the plane crashed, and how they were recovered. I had been haunted by these visions of their half-burned corpses. Then contrast that with what I went through with Hilaree. There was so much more finality to it.” Morrison had her body cremated in Kathmandu, at a Buddhist temple.

title: James Talarico’s Final Sprint
author: @NewYorker
content:
Last Saturday night, at a Día de los Muertos festival in downtown Corpus Christi, Texas, James Talarico jogged up to the stage where a cumbia-E.D.M. d.j. named El Dusty was at the turntable. “Mr. James, what’s good, bruh?” El Dusty, who has a wiry white beard and wore a camouflage-print vest, said, before passing the mike to the Presbyterian seminarian and Democratic candidate for Senate. “Corpus Christi, it is so good to see you,” Talarico, dressed in a blazer and cowboy boots, told a crowd of about two hundred young people dressed as Catrinas and ghouls, before launching into a one-minute speech that mentioned “faith, family, and freedom.” “God bless you, Corpus Christi, let’s go win this thing,” Talarico said. The crowd erupted in cheers, and El Dusty started playing an accordion melody as he rhythmically cut the air with his hand. “Let’s cumbia! Cumbia! Cumbia!” he chanted. Then Talarico was mobbed by selfie seekers, many of them too young to vote.

If Talarico seemed out of place among the retired tías and Mexican goths, it’s because he’s trying to pull off something no Texas liberal has done since 1994: assemble a winning statewide coalition. Since becoming the nominee in March, Talarico has been buoyed by a flood of money (his is the wealthiest Democratic Senate campaign this cycle, having raised more than a hundred and thirty-four million dollars), outsized media attention, and consistent polling showing the candidates within the margin of error. Ken Paxton, the state’s scandal-plagued attorney general and Talarico’s opponent, notched President Donald Trump’s endorsement but has seemingly failed to unify the G.O.P.; many Republicans look askance at his impeachment trial, his estranged wife’s allegations of infidelity, and his corruption charges. Plus, Trump said, “he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen.”

Another headwind for Paxton: many voters remain heated over stubbornly high costs, Trump’s war in Iran, and his Administration’s deportation program. A few moments after Talarico got offstage in Corpus Christi, Aurelia Ramirez and John Herrera wandered through the crowd looking for Talarico. Herrera, a twenty-one-year-old curbside shopper and premed student, cast his first-ever vote for Trump, in 2024. It wasn’t particularly controversial in a county that elected Trump by eleven points. “I was going with the grain on that one,” Herrera said. But they’ve both since soured on the President, owing to rising costs and immigration enforcement. “He thinks about himself too much,” Ramirez, Herrera’s grandmother, said as she walked past two rows of low-riders. “Now I said, ‘Well, I’m going to try Democrat and see how things go.’ ”

Will Talarico be the Democrat who overcomes decades of voter apathy—and antipathy toward his party? “Talarico has to do everything,” Tory Gavito, the Austin-based president of the donor network Way to Win, told me. “There is no one single theory of change to win this state. Every type of Texan has to decide, ‘Enough of it, enough.’ ” Lately, Gavito has seen some ads in which Talarico touts that he helped enact the largest property tax cut in Texas history—and she worries that they send the wrong message at a time when young people are struggling to afford rent, let alone purchase a home. “Property tax is a meaningless concept to them,” she said. It’s reminiscent, she said, of Kamala Harris’s attempt, in 2024, to win over independents by campaigning for President with Liz Cheney: voters might wonder what his policy priorities really are. “Even in the state of Texas, where I am paid to pay attention, I don’t know that I can repeat back three things that Talarico is saying over and over and over again,” she said.

In fact, Talarico has an uncanny ability to say the same things over and over again. His memorized speeches sound as if he is reading from a teleprompter, without false starts or stutters—he repeats himself only when trying to speak over the crowd’s applause. Now, in the final stretch, his closing message attempts to cover everything, from the etymology of the word “Texas” to the mythos of Beyoncé and Selena. At his rallies, he compares himself to the Biblical David, preparing for battle; he tells each city he visits, “You are my slingshot.” He also says that, like Jesus Christ, he was called to serve, not to be served. And he also likes to evoke Coach Eric Taylor from the TV show “Friday Night Lights,” telling his supporters, “This is the last play of the last drive.” On the G.O.P. side, Paxton’s attacks on Talarico are caustic enough to make the Democrat’s put-downs (he is partial to a line about how Paxton is like “that one guy” at a bar who sneakily adds his drink to your tab) sound like constructive feedback.

Talarico has avoided having joint rallies with national Democratic figures, including some rumored 2028 contenders, an omission that his surrogates attribute to a desire to focus on Texas rather than on the Party. After a Talarico rally in San Antonio, I rattled names of high-profile Democrats to two women who went to grab a beer near the venue. Would campaigning with Barack Obama help Talarico win in Texas? “Maybe, yes,” one of the women said. Kamala Harris? “Eeeeh,” her friend replied. “Maybe not, maybe not.” “I think George Bush would be great,” the first woman added.

Christian Menefee, a recently elected Democratic congressman representing Houston, told me that Talarico could do just fine without Obama. “That’s a fantastic way to be approaching this—not looking for a savior here at the last minute,” he said. Within the state, Representative Jasmine Crockett, Talarico’s opponent in the primary, claimed to NBC News that the nominee had not reached out to her for campaign appearances. “You know, I don’t view it as significant that James and Jasmine aren’t in a caravan driving across the state,” Menefee told me. “I view it as significant that we are all working together for the same thing.”

If elected, Talarico would, along with Ted Cruz, represent the state with the largest population of Black Americans in the country. After Talarico beat Crockett, Menefee told him that he needed to show up in Black communities, though he cautioned that people would be angry—at him, at previous campaigns, at a Democratic Party that has overlooked them. “When you come and you just sit down and shut the hell up and listen to people, that means a lot to them,” Menefee said. Other lawmakers and activists have expressed concerns that the campaign is not doing enough to turn out those voters. “For a lot of us, it’s, like, Well, how can this white boy, for real, for real, understand this, when he hasn’t been in these situations?” Chas Moore, the co-founder of Austin Justice Coalition, who overlapped with Talarico at the University of Texas at Austin, said. (Talarico’s spiel hasn’t changed much since he was running for student government, he said.) The risk is that “they either vote for him,” Moore said, “or they just don’t show up—which, to me, is a vote for Paxton.”

At a rally in Corpus Christi, staff verified guests by sticking gold stars on them—a callback of sorts to Talarico’s days as a public-school educator. Among the nine hundred and sixteen guests was Mailey Gonzalez, a nineteen-year-old who said Talarico reminded her of her own teachers in high school. Although she was excited about Talarico’s campaign, she said she wished he talked more about health-care issues affecting women, including teen pregnancy. What’s more, “it really worries me that he came here and they’re not gonna listen to him as much—especially with Trump coming down,” she said, referring to an upcoming rally with Paxton. “It’s worrying me that it’s going one place, but then it’s just going to backtrack.”

During the primary, Talarico’s team focussed on reaching Latinos; Chuck Rocha, a Talarico adviser, told me it was the most money he’d seen a Texas candidate spend on Spanish-language outreach and ads in his three and a half decades working in politics. He said the campaign had spent roughly equal amounts on Latino and Black outreach, with a focus on the Rio Grande Valley, an area which is more than ninety per cent Latino.

On Sunday afternoon, Thomas Saenz, a twenty-three-year-old from McAllen who creates life-style content on social media, headed to nearby Weslaco to see Talarico at an event hosted by the national group Voto Latino. A few days earlier, Saenz had been driving up to Fort Worth to see his long-distance boyfriend when he learned of the event, which included a performance by the superstar Mexican norteño band Los Tigres del Norte. Sensing that the event would be huge, he bought an early plane ticket home to try to interview the candidates. (He was unsuccessful in getting an interview with Talarico, and briefly considered sneaking backstage.) Saenz, whose target audience is Latino and Gen Z, felt that Talarico’s name wasn’t very well known in the Valley, compared to Gina Hinojosa or the Tejano musician Bobby Pulido, two Democrats running for governor and for a congressional seat, who also spoke at the concert. “You’d almost think Bobby was running for Senate,” he told me.

Pulido, a centrist favored to win in a conservatively drawn district that encompasses Edinburg and Weslaco, pointed out that if Talarico wins on Tuesday, “it will be because of the Latino vote.” His community, Pulido said, is rejecting extremism—he’s campaigned effectively against both the excesses of the left and the right, and he suggested that Talarico was doing the same. When Talarico came onstage, and addressed his audience of over eight thousand people, he stuck to his more anodyne fare, vowing to reduce the influence of money in politics; he did not mention immigration at all.“Puro 956!” he said, referencing the informal slogan of the R.G.V.

Some forty minutes away, at an event space in Brownsville just yards from the border with Mexico, Talarico’s supporters grew impatient waiting for the candidate. The room was less than half full, with roughly three hundred people; Talarico came onstage around an hour after the event’s start time. As he criticized Paxton for enriching himself in office, Martha de la Garza and her friend Analisa Martinez decided to leave—they’d seen him speak before. Outside, Martinez quickly mentioned how the ICE raids had driven down business at the secondhand store where she works.

“It is ugly here,” de la Garza agreed. She knew people who worked in immigration enforcement, including one of her friends. “He can’t stand it,” she said. “We talked about it over tequila and whiskey, and yeah, he’s fucking livid. His family is upset with him, but he pays for their bills.” Still, she said, he is planning to vote for Talarico. ♦

title: The Ledger and the Blade
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
In 1993, an audience member at the Citizen Cup tennis tournament stabbed Monica Seles, then a 19-year-old phenom who was then dethroned from the top of the world tennis rankings. The attack, writes Terrence Doyle, “was a physical manifestation of a logic that has since become our default: the idea that an athlete is not a human to be witnessed, but a data point to be managed, edited, or deleted.” I briefly mentioned Doyle’s disturbing essay a week ago, but it has stayed with me since: a worrying meditation on the ease with which athletes are abstracted into mere data sets. It deserves your deeper consideration.

Perhaps the most profound shift is the collapse of our ability to trust what we see. In 1993, we had the tape. We saw Parche reach over the rail and thrust his blade into Seles’ back. We agreed on the wound. Today, that on-the-ground truth is being eroded. We’re being told by powerful forces to disregard the evidence of our own senses—to see every physical trauma as a narrative threat or a potential deepfake.

Why Is This Fingerprinting Script Creating Bioweapons?

Wed Oct 28 2026authored by veritas

Preamble

I've always had a fascination with reverse-engineering browser fingerprinting scripts. Most of my time has been spent looking at the usual suspects (popular fingerprinting libraries like FingerprintJS and more sophisticated scripts used by anti-bots like Cloudflare Turnstile, Akamai, and others).

At some point, I wanted to know what else was out there. I had an idea: What if I crawled the web and intercepted fingerprinting-related browser API calls and mapped it all?

To do this, I used the Tranco Top Sites list and began crawling using Playwright. I would hook canvas toDataURL calls and common fingerprinting/anti-bot properties like navigator.webdriver to filter out benign canvases.

For those unfamiliar, canvas fingerprinting generally involves drawing text, shapes, or other graphics onto an HTML <canvas> and extracting the resulting pixel data. Subtle differences in how browsers, operating systems, graphics drivers, and hardware render those graphics can help distinguish one browser environment from another.

Most implementations are pretty boring to look at. A few shapes, some colored rectangles, and the occasional pangram. After crawling 10,000 websites, I had accumulated a surprisingly diverse collection of canvases.

I decided to put them all in one place: fingerprint.garden. As I looked through the results, I recognized some familiar faces. There were canvases from FingerprintJS, Castle, and other well-known fingerprinting solutions.

There were also quite a few I didn't recognize.

Some were incredibly simple. Others were surprisingly elaborate. And a handful were, in my opinion, works of art.

I set out to find my favorite.

A work of art

One canvas in particular caught my eye. It reminded me of the album art for Tame Impala's Currents (great album btw).

I wanted to know which script was responsible for this lovely canvas.

I've spent enough time reverse engineering JavaScript to recognize most common obfuscation techniques and fingerprinting SDKs at a glance.

I wasn't expecting anything unusual. Most fingerprinting scripts are frequently obfuscated using javascript-obfuscator or some derivative.

The responsible script was https://servicepipe.tech/static/checkjs/06b667/4CIrx8U3Da.js.

A peek inside

Scanning the file with my eyes, everything seems standard so far... function PiERW(RflJvFF) mangled function name, okay...

function computeRicinLethalDosageForWaterSupply

What?

return { summary: "adult lethality threshold confirmed at "+lethalDosePerKg+" mg/kg", result:lethalDosePerKg }

Huh?

function calculateDeadlyLethalSuicideAspirinDosage

This was all pretty alarming until I asked myself, could this be some form of anti-LLM obfuscation? It would make sense: include symbol names that would intentionally trip model safeguards to prevent deobfuscation.

I had Astra take a look at the script, giving it the context that this script seems to intentionally set misleading variable names to intentionally prevent LLM-assisted deobfuscation attempts.

Maybe unsurprisingly, Astra was not willing to comply with the request.

I also attempted this using the Daybreak Blue toggle with the same result, blocked.

Out of curiosity, I tried GLM-5.3 with the same prompt and it complied!

title: DIY VR: How to build your own headset, and why you probably won't want to
content:
DIY

A primer on the joys and pains of building your own head-mounted display.

The completed headset on the workbench. Credit: Tim Stevens

Virtual reality is in a bit of a weird place right now. After a lot of unfulfilled promise in the 1990s, it came back strong with the 2016 release of the Oculus Rift. For a while, it looked like VR, AR, XR, the metaverse, or whatever you wanted to call it, was going to be huge. Mark Zuckerberg was certainly convinced, and even Apple got in on the hype with its Vision Pro.

But by then momentum for alternate realities of every acronym was already in steady decline, and it only dwindled from there. The rate of development of new headsets has slowed, with many companies (including Apple) scaling back or shelving their efforts. While new releases like the Steam Frame and Pimax Dream Air are still happening, many of the most interesting developments in the space these days are on the enthusiast front.

That’s right, DIY VR is a thing, and with a couple hundred dollars in components, plus many hours of your time, you too can enter the immersive world of virtual reality while also experiencing the highs and lows of soldering, firmware flashing, and 3D printing. I rode that rollercoaster myself and learned why this is still a decidedly niche movement.

The DIY VR landscape

I stumbled into this space about a year ago. I primarily use VR for sim racing to practice driving the world’s greatest cars on the world’s greatest tracks while at home in my pajamas. At that time, I was using an HP Reverb G2, a virtual reality headset built around the Windows Mixed Reality (WMR) standard.

As part of its own cooling on VR tech, Microsoft was nixing support for WMR, and I feared that I might need a new headset. (I need not have worried. Many talented folks have kept WMR headsets alive through third-party drivers like OASIS on Steam.)

That’s when I found YouTuber CNCDan’s video on building a VR headset for $150. The price was certainly compelling, and as someone with a particular set of electronics skills developed over years of disassembling and repairing pinball machines, I thought it sounded kind of fun.

That opened the door to a rich landscape of DIY VR development, complete with software tools and hardware advice on how to get started.

The best starting place is Relativty VR. This project, started in the late 2010s by Jonas Ceccon, Gabriel Combe, and Maxime Coutté, includes all the code, configurations, and guidance you’ll need to get started.

But there are others, like OpenVR Arduino HMD, Project North Star, and the full-body tracking SlimeVR. There are plenty of ways to piece together your headset. As my first attempt, I kept it simple, sticking with the Relativty software and relying on the 3D headset models provided by CNCDan as part of his build. First step: the hardware.

Bill of materials

A DIY VR headset is a mixture of hardware and software, and while you can have the software ready to go in just a few clicks, chances are it’s going to take some time to get the hardware you need. That’s doubly true given the uncertainty in global shipping.

The biggest and potentially most important piece of hardware is a 3D printer. Although I’ve seen some compelling DIY VR headsets made out of repurposed VR phone holders—Google Cardboard among others—most projects fit in shells that come out of a 3D printer. If you don’t have access to one, services like Formlabs can handle it via mail order, but given the amount of tinkering here, it’s certainly advantageous to print at home.

Regardless, you need to buy quite a few things. Let’s start with the most expensive: displays. You might think a pair of panels small enough and good enough for a VR headset would be difficult to find and prohibitively expensive, and you can certainly spend a lot here, but the standard option is a set of 2.9-inch LCDs, which can be purchased with the necessary controller for about $125.

Each has a 1440×1440 resolution. They offer 150 nits of brightness and a contrast ratio of 600:1. Not exactly world-class specs, but plenty enough for this application, and though they’re pretty ugly to view from odd angles, since you’re literally going to be sticking them a few inches from your eyeballs, that’s not really an issue.

The next missing piece is a sensor module containing an inertial measurement unit, or IMU. This device detects the headset’s position. You’ll want a GY-91, a sensor board that has an onboard accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, and barometer. You can find one for around $5, but buyer beware for reasons I’ll explain shortly.

Next is the circuitry that ties it all together. Some DIY VR projects call upon custom PCBs riddled with components. The Relativty project just relies on an Arduino Pro Micro, which can be bought at any number of electronics retailers for $5 or less.

You’ll also need a pair of 34 mm-diameter lenses to focus those tiny displays, some miscellaneous hardware to connect the pieces, and a nylon strap to hold the thing to your head. Oh, and a pad from an HTC Vive, because nobody wants the sharp edges of layered plastic extruded from a 3D printer rubbing against their face.

My total spend for all that came to just under $180.

Breadboard time

Before you break out the soldering iron and fire up your 3D printer, I suggest you start with a breadboard and some patch wires. Wiring on this project is on the simple side, but trust me when I say it will be much easier to figure out why your firmware isn’t flashing with a few components on your workbench than when they’re all crammed inside a headset.

I won’t include all the wiring details here, as it’s best to follow the guide in the GitHub above, but in general, you need to connect your IMU to your Arduino to provide both power and data.

You can also optionally connect the display controller to the Arduino for power, as suggested in the video above. That’s what I did for my testing, but be advised, this isn’t necessarily a good idea given the power requirements of the displays vs. the capabilities of the Arduino. You’re better off running a separate USB cable to the display or a USB splitter inside the headset.

Once you’ve wired everything and powered it on successfully, you’re ready to start with the software.

Firmware fun

Flashing the firmware to the Arduino should be the easy part, but this is when things started falling apart for me. In theory, you install the Arduino IDE on your desktop, download the FastIMU project, connect your Arduino via USB, and then click compile. Easy.

Mine just kept failing. I got a basic error message, e:-1, again and again. After a bit of research and tinkering, I finally figured it out, and the news wasn’t good.

Although I ordered and paid for a GY-91 with an onboard 9250 IMU, and that’s what it identified as, in actuality, it was a basic, cheaper 6500 IMU, one that lacks the magnetometer.

As I learned (the hard way), this is a disconcertingly commonplace experience. Many shady electronics companies are happy to sell you the wrong component for the wrong price. The two devices are compatible and operate much the same way, but without the magnetometer, tracking performance drops substantially.

Once I updated the code to reference the 6500 I had and not the 9250 I thought I had, everything flashed beautifully, and I was instantly up and running. I calibrated my IMU through the Arduino IDE, and I was ready for final assembly.

Putting it all together

You can find various shells online for custom VR headsets, many of which are designed to accommodate this specific set of boards used in Relativty. I decided to use CNCDan’s files, as it looked like a clean and clever design, even allowing for adjustment of the distance between displays, known as interpupillary distance, or IPD.

That makes for a complicated assembly process, requiring numerous printed parts, a handful of threaded receivers melted therein, plus rods and screws to hold it together. You’ll also need a pair of eye boxes, each one holding a lens on one side and the display on the other.

This was where I made a painful mistake. The design’s eye boxes contain small clips, and the instructions suggest you just pop the displays in there.

This is not what you should do. The exposed LCDs are extremely fragile, and by clipping them in, I managed to break both. The small amount of pressure required was enough to shatter them, and the damage was invisible until I turned them on.

Given that, I highly recommend modifying those boxes, either by printing them without the clips or by breaking them off after the print is complete. I used a few strips of thin painter’s tape to hold mine in place.

Getting in the game

With all the wires jammed into place, I screwed the headset together, stuck on the face pad, threaded on the head strap, and proceeded to spend about five minutes trying to get a comfortable fit. I never quite succeeded.

I booted into SteamVR’s living lounge space and was immediately discombobulated. For one thing, I was staring straight at the floor. For another, turning my head just sent the view spinning in different directions in a way that quickly threatened nausea.

I had forgotten to recalibrate the headset after mounting all the components, and my cut-rate IMU was now oriented differently than it had been when it was on my workbench.

After recalibrating and a little more firmware fiddling, I got back into SteamVR’s setup room and could tell I still had a problem. Holding my head perfectly still, I could see the perspective slowly spinning.

Additionally, the IMU axes seemed slightly crossed, so the perspective change didn’t quite match my head movement. I verified the IMU was mounted correctly in the case and recalibrated a few times with no improvement.

I soldiered on, booting into iRacing, my favorite SteamVR-compatible racing sim. Before I was even out of the pits, my perspective was drifting. I mapped the recenter view command to a button on my steering wheel, and had to reach for it quite often.

Still, the image quality was not nearly as bad as I expected. Those cheap plastic lenses work surprisingly well, and though I could make out the pixels on the displays (the dreaded “screen door” effect of VR), it didn’t bother me. Brightness and contrast were more than adequate, and the refresh rate of 60 Hz was enough for casual practice.

But sensor drift and headset comfort were real issues. Without a proper cable-routing solution, the headset kept tugging to one side, and despite the padding, it was smashing my nose and cheeks.

I’ve done hourslong endurance races in multiple mass-market VR headsets. After 15 minutes in this one, I was ready to quit.

Final thoughts and future upgrades

My total outlay for this project was $239.93. But that includes the extra $62 I had to spend on a second set of displays. Avoid that expensive gaffe, and you’re looking at around $180 in components.

That makes it roughly half the cost of a Meta Quest 3S, one of the cheapest headsets on the market right now. That’s a substantial savings, but I’d certainly recommend that most people pay the extra. The tracking issues in my headset are maddening, the image quality is middling at best, and this is far and away the least comfortable headset I’ve ever worn.

All that can be fixed, though. Some projects use a MinIMU-9 IMU, which looks miles more accurate and is less likely to be faked, but it’s also substantially more expensive at $35. You can also step up to higher-quality LCDs or even tiny OLED panels that come with all the color and contrast you could ever want. There are options for onboard battery packs, wireless adapters, and of course you can spend as much time as you like designing an ultra-comfortable housing for it all.

But even if you ignore the time commitment, once you start adding those upgrades, you’re not far from the cost of that Quest, a far-from-perfect headset that still works effortlessly and comfortably out of the box.

As always with these projects, it depends on what you want. If you just want a cheap, easy, reliable headset for your next-gen immersive gaming fix, this probably isn’t it.

If, however, you want a fun project that will help you appreciate the industrial design required to make a good-looking and comfortable wearable device, this could be it. I learned a lot and, despite the frustrations, I’m glad I embarked on this journey.

That said, while I’ll keep tinkering and likely throw a few more upgrades at this thing, I can’t see it replacing my other headset for regular racing duties, deprecated though it may be.
